source.title: Data-Efficient Double-Win Lottery Tickets from Robust Pre-training
source.authors: Tian-Long Chen; Zhenyu (Allen) Zhang; Sijia Liu; Yang Zhang; Shi-Yu Chang; Zhang-Yang Wang

record.file_problem: none; the supplied text includes the paper and appendices, though some figure/table layouts are flattened
record.tranche_reason: The study reports how sparse subnetworks transfer to held-out downstream data, but it does not test any listed version: it does not study random-label memorization, width, convolution versus fully connected architecture, optimizer or batch comparisons, dropout, magnitude-aware sharpness, or removal of memorized examples.
record.gate_note: The paper reports standard and robust test accuracy for pruned subnetworks across datasets, training regimes, and sparsity levels. Several additional results appear only in figures; rows below cover the explicit textual results that can be tied to a setting without reconstructing figure values. Cited results from prior work were excluded.
record.test_reason: The study measures sparse pretrained subnetworks' downstream accuracy and robustness, without testing any listed claim version. Its loss-landscape visualizations use test loss and do not measure magnitude-aware training sharpness or training–test gaps required by V7. Pruning weights does not test V2's width claim or V8's removal of memorized training examples.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate: the authors conclude that double-win subnetworks from robust pretraining retain strong standard and robust transfer performance and improve data efficiency. Fast adversarial pretraining can be preferable at intermediate sparsity with limited data, while adversarial pretraining dominates at higher sparsity. Their investigations are confined to computer vision.
record.recipe_differences: Uses iterative magnitude pruning of ImageNet-pretrained ResNet-50 weights, then evaluates downstream transfer under standard and adversarial training; it does not use the original claim's random-label memorization setup.
record.method_sensitivity: Pre-training type, downstream dataset, downstream training regime, sparsity, and downstream training-data fraction change the reported performance.

fits_no_version.finding: Sparse pretrained ResNet-50 subnetworks can match dense models across standard and adversarial downstream training. Matching sparsity depends on dataset and pretraining.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Appropriately selected pretrained sparse subnetworks can retain dense models' downstream accuracy and robustness.

fits_no_version.finding: Under limited downstream data, fast adversarial pretraining can outperform adversarial pretraining at intermediate sparsities; adversarial pretraining overtakes at higher sparsity. On SVHN, both can lose their advantage over standard pretraining at sufficiently high sparsity.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The transfer advantage of robust pretraining depends on its strength, subnetwork sparsity, and downstream data availability.

fits_no_version.finding: Transfer-attack accuracy increases from 55.54% for the dense model to 62.79%, 60.09%, and 56.49% at the three tested nonzero sparsities.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Selected sparse subnetworks from adversarial pretraining can improve transfer-attack accuracy over their dense counterpart.

fits_no_version.finding: At 73.79% sparsity, test-loss contour visualizations show flatter basins for fast adversarial pretraining, accompanying better data-limited transfer accuracy.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Test-loss landscape geometry may help explain differences in sparse subnetworks' transfer performance.

record.peer_reviewed: International Conference on Machine Learning, PMLR 162, 2022
record.problems: Exact downstream accuracy curves are mainly presented in figures; the prose reports extrema and qualitative comparisons rather than a full per-setting numeric breakdown. Several sparsity extrema are not fully mapped to datasets and metrics in the prose. Experiments are limited to computer vision.
record.rows_left_out: Figure-only accuracy values from Figures 3–5 and A10 were not transcribed because the text provides no exact values and the flattened figure material does not support reliable extraction. Figure 6 and Figure A9 loss-contour visualizations were not recorded as sharpness-generalization results because the study does not measure the magnitude-aware sharpness in V7 or quantify a training-test gap.

untested.parts: Random-label fitting and comparison with natural-label held-out accuracy under the same architecture and recipe.
Widening networks beyond the width needed for zero training error and measuring subsequent test error.
Convolutional versus fully connected networks and the contribution of local connectivity.
Adaptive versus SGD optimizers, tuning scope, and optimizer modifications.
Batch-size comparisons under fixed epoch budgets and adaptations that reduce large-batch penalties.
Dropout effects across data sizes, dropout strengths, and augmentation conditions.
Magnitude-aware perturbation tolerance measured on training data, its association with training–test gaps, and comparison with norm- and margin-based measures.
Removing examples selected by label memorization and comparing retrained test accuracy with equal-size random removal.

record.verdict_notes: States are cannot_determine relative to V1–V8 because no row measures a listed effect; this does not negate the reported transfer findings. No missing result bearing on a listed version was found.

versions.untested_parts: Random-label memorization and held-out natural-label accuracy under the same recipe.
Width sweeps past the interpolation threshold.
Convolutional versus fully connected architecture comparisons.
Adaptive versus SGD optimizer comparisons and tuning.
Large-batch versus small-batch comparisons under fixed epoch budgets.
Magnitude-aware sharpness and its relationship to the training-test gap.
Removing examples identified as memorized and measuring the effect on test accuracy.

rows.subject: ResNet-50 subnetworks from standard pre-training θSTD, fast adversarial pre-training θFAT, and adversarial pre-training θAT
rows.size_stated: ResNet-50; subnetworks with reported sparsity levels
rows.stage_stated: ImageNet pre-training followed by downstream transfer
rows.operation_detail: IMP subnetworks transferred with standard training; paper reports standard test accuracy
rows.baseline: unpruned dense network; matching is defined as within one standard deviation
rows.value: The text states double-win tickets generally exist and have unimpaired performance; it gives extreme sparsity levels of 89.26%, 89.26%, and 91.41% for the three pre-training types, respectively, but does not fully disambiguate each value's dataset and metric in the prose.
rows.uncertainty: mean and standard deviation are reported; numerical uncertainty not stated in prose
rows.note: Qualitative claim and sparsity values are reported in prose; exact test-accuracy values are figure-only.
rows.check: The sparsities are misassigned to training regimes. Section 4.1 identifies 89.26%, 89.26%, and 91.41% as CIFAR-10 double-win thresholds for standard, fast adversarial, and adversarial pretraining, respectively, jointly satisfying all required metrics and regimes. These are selection thresholds, not accuracy values. The row aggregates datasets and pretraining conditions and compares the study's subnetworks with dense models; it measures no listed version.

rows.subject: ResNet-50 subnetworks from standard pre-training θSTD, fast adversarial pre-training θFAT, and adversarial pre-training θAT
rows.size_stated: ResNet-50; subnetworks with reported sparsity levels
rows.stage_stated: ImageNet pre-training followed by downstream transfer
rows.operation_detail: IMP subnetworks transferred with adversarial training; paper reports standard and robust test accuracy
rows.baseline: unpruned dense network; matching is defined as within one standard deviation
rows.value: The text states double-win tickets generally exist and gives sparsity levels of 73.79%, 79.03%, and 83.22% for the three pre-training types, respectively; it does not fully disambiguate each value's dataset and metric in the prose.
rows.uncertainty: mean and standard deviation are reported; numerical uncertainty not stated in prose
rows.note: Exact test-accuracy values are figure-only. The paper also says subnetworks from adversarial pre-training outperform those from fast adversarial and standard pre-training across the three downstream tasks.
rows.check: The 73.79%, 79.03%, and 83.22% sparsities are CIFAR-100 double-win thresholds for the three pretraining types, not thresholds specific to adversarial downstream training. The corresponding SVHN thresholds are 0%, 79.03%, and 96.48%. These thresholds jointly cover both training regimes and required metrics. Split accuracy results by dataset, pretraining, and measure if retained as findings outside the listed versions.

rows.subject: ResNet-50 subnetworks from standard pre-training θSTD, fast adversarial pre-training θFAT, and adversarial pre-training θAT
rows.size_stated: ResNet-50; subnetworks with reported sparsity levels
rows.stage_stated: ImageNet pre-training followed by data-limited downstream transfer
rows.operation_detail: IMP subnetworks transferred with adversarial training using a limited fraction of downstream training data
rows.baseline: θAT subnetworks at middle sparsity levels
rows.value: At middle sparsity levels, θFAT subnetworks show improvements over θAT of up to {30.97%, 2.42%, 10.05%} SA and {8.36%, 0.70%, 18.49%} RA for CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and SVHN, respectively; at larger sparsity, θAT overtakes θFAT.
rows.note: Reported maxima combine the 10% and 1% settings; the prose does not assign each maximum to a particular data fraction.
rows.check: The reported maxima and crossover agree with Section 5, but combine datasets, data fractions, sparsities, and two measures. This is a comparison of pretraining variants outside the listed versions; its crossover does not establish a partial effect for any version.

rows.subject: ResNet-50 subnetworks from fast adversarial pre-training θFAT and adversarial pre-training θAT
rows.stage_stated: ImageNet pre-training followed by data-limited downstream transfer
rows.operation_detail: IMP subnetworks transferred with limited downstream training data
rows.baseline: θSTD subnetworks at the same stated setting
rows.value: The performance of θFAT and θAT degrades to θSTD's level at large sparsity 83.22% and 97.19%, respectively.
rows.note: The prose does not specify which of 10% or 1% corresponds to each cited sparsity.
rows.check: Section 5 assigns 83.22% and 97.19% sparsity to fast adversarial and adversarial pretraining, respectively. It does not assign these thresholds separately to the 10% and 1% data conditions. Loss of their advantage over standard pretraining measures none of the listed effects.

rows.subject: ResNet-50 subnetworks from adversarial pre-training θAT
rows.stage_stated: ImageNet pre-training followed by CIFAR-10 adversarial training
rows.operation_detail: Evaluated under transfer attack from an unseen robust model

conditions.value: transfer attack from an unseen robust model

rows.value: 89.26% at 0% sparsity; 93.13% at 89.26% sparsity; 95.60% at 93.13% sparsity; 56.49% at 95.60% sparsity
rows.note: The paper describes sparse subnetworks as consistently outperforming the dense counterpart under transfer attack; row records the table values as labeled.
rows.check: Table A2 was misread. Transfer-attack accuracies at 0%, 89.26%, 93.13%, and 95.60% sparsity are 55.54%, 62.79%, 60.09%, and 56.49%, respectively. Corresponding robust accuracies are 47.11%, 56.00%, 60.05%, and 50.85%. The row mistakenly treats sparsity entries as accuracies. This sparse-versus-dense method comparison measures no listed version.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.
